Messages.Author: jspektr
Messages.Body:
There was a lot of talk about the new Cam vampires having a much
better costing structure than older vampires, and of the 15 new
library cards in the set. That being said, I'm wondering if anyone's
seen a significant shift to using the new cards compared to old cards.

Even though several of our players in St. Louis are buying Cam, very
few of them have been using any of it. Most of our new players have
been concentrating on buying Sabbat War and Final Nights, which are
hard to find at local shops, and ignoring Cam. When asked, they say
the cards they want aren't in the Cam set.

Why might this be? I was thinking that perhaps it is because none of
the new cards in the Cam set are actually compelling enough to make
people need to buy them. While it is good for the game to come out
with a new set that can be completely ignored and not have it impact
your competitiveness, I think that it's not so good for sales. If the
15 new cards, or some of the vampires, had been significantly better
than the old stuff, I think it would have sold better because you
would have to buy Camarilla cards or lose your edge to those that did.

Do you find the Cam set gives you a significant advantage over players
that don't have it, or does it make no difference?

JSpektr

I find this a completely silly question to frame in this way. Clearly,
due to the makeup of Camarilla edition, it's a complete apples and
oranges comparison to juxtapose sales of expansions like Sabbat War and
Final Nights with CE and ask if the meaning of differing numbers could
relate to the play value of the cards. That ignores all the issues of
grouping vampires and the vast majority of reprints in CE library cards.
I'm not sure how you could miss these points and the obvious implications
they're going to have on sales.

To be sure, I do find several interesting issues in the makeup of
Camarilla edition. For instance, was it reasonable, let alone a good
thing, to reprint most of the library cards while inventing an entirely
new set of vampires? (My opinion: no. That was bad.) Is it a good
thing to sprinkle a *few* new library cards in amongst a bunch of
reprinted library cards? (Again, my opinion is no. This was done in
Sabbat War, as well, and both times it created a very awkward situation
with respect to highly demanded new cards in amongst reprints that are
only somewhat valuable to a subset of the population. However, I'm not
unsympathetic with why White Wolf might be tempted to do that. I wish
they'd at least refrain from making any new cards rare in this kind of
a situation, though.) Should some of the new cards have been put in
precons? (My opinion is yes, as long as no new card is issued *only*
in precons, which creates another awkward situation.) However, none of
these issues can properly be analyzed by comparing CE sales to other
expansions. And the existence of such issues highlights why a
comparison of sales between CE and other expansions is itself orthogonal
to questions of comparing the play values of the cards from each issue.

I haven't had any chances to use the new cards so far, Jyhad play in
Phoenix is so dismal nowadays. I wouldn't venture an assessment of
vampires at all. My superficial look at the library cards reveals a
mixed bag: apparently useless Abandoning the Flesh to Tensions in the
Ranks which is a surefire addition to certain kinds of popular existing
decks. Baltimore Purge and High Ground come to mind as cards that have
specific enough uses that you'll certainly see them in decks but not
likely all that often. At this stage, I imagine most of the new cards
are just being mildly experimented with and no one's found any real
burning advantages in them yet. There's probably no killer or true
staple cards amongst them. But given how they've been printed, I don't
think I'd want there to be. That, by itself, is going to necessarily
limit a huge rush on people bothering to buy CE boosters who don't need
them for the reprints.

> While it is good for the game to come out
> with a new set that can be completely ignored and not have it impact
> your competitiveness, I think that it's not so good for sales. If the
> 15 new cards, or some of the vampires, had been significantly better
> than the old stuff, I think it would have sold better because you
> would have to buy Camarilla cards or lose your edge to those that did.

It's hard for you or I to really have a worthwhile perspective on what
any given level of sales of CE did for or to the game, directly due
to player response or indirectly due to White Wolf's financial incentive
to issue future expansions. We don't even know whether the current
level of sales are viewed as bad or good by White Wolf or whether they
were foreseen or not, whatever they are.

I always assumed CE was not going to be hot seller from the start nor
thought anyone should expect it to be. The concept always seemed to be
a long-range proposition: have a "base set" in print of which White
Wolf controlled the contents. A base set, which is still available by
mail order if not often found on retailer's shelves, already existed.
In fact, two exist: Jyhad and the second VtES edition. Given that
point, I'm not sure CE was ever likely to fly off shelves, at least at
first. I've always assumed, therefore, that White Wolf had strategic
reasons for bringing it out that they had carefully considered. If so,
any debate about it here would take place in a huge vacuum of
information.

Fred

A good question, and one I would have to answer "No" to at the moment.

My theory is this is largely a familiarity issue. When thinking of new
decks, I have been sticking to what I know at the moment, and I can
only guess this is also the case for other folk in my locale. To be
honest, I have a modicum of Camerilla, but can't reliably remember
names or abilities the new folk at all. A few have seeped into my
subconcious, but by far the minority.

<snip>

> Do you find the Cam set gives you a significant advantage over players
> that don't have it, or does it make no difference?

Well, as far as the "big fellas" go, yes, there is a percieved
advantage. The abilities feel stronger and the skills meld better for
key strategies. This is, however, frequently offset by the lack of
"cheap" or efficient titles OTHER than Primogen.

However, the small to mid-caps feel weaker. Compare the likes of Anvil
and the 7 - 8 cap Ventrue Princes to the new equivalent. Yes, nowhere
near as broken, but also significantly less powerful. There seems to
be a hang up in giving the new vamps OOC disciplines, which (on the
whole) weakens the mix. Yes, they are great for interesting new decks,
but cause issues for basic, clan focused decks.

The key exception to all of the above is the Tremere. Their selection
accross the board is stronger than most other clans - especially in
the 4 cap and below range, where they have a great selection of
Thau-heavy vampires in groups 2 and 3 - and there are some stand-out
great vampires (even an 8 cap Justicar!!!). That and the fact that
they have dominate, now have enhanced combat skills, and have more
ways of getting around Strike: Combat ends than any other clan
(in-clan, they can stop the most common forms of S:CE by using one of
4 cards, plus one has a special: this is much better than most clans
options in this field) means that they are totally a force to be
reckoned with. We have seen a significant rise in their use, almost
since the day of release of the Cam set.

DH

The new Vampires aren't necessarily better in the 2-7 point range, but for
vampires who are 8+, they are noticably better (in terms of how much "stuff"
they got). The 2-7 point vampires are using, mostly, the same pricing
structure, except in terms of +1 bleed and +1 strength, both of which are
cheaper now than they were when Jyhad came out.

Certain clans are better off now than they used to be, however--the mid
range Nosferatu (5-7) are *much* better than they used to be, as the
original 5-7 point Nosferatu were, mostly, ass. The Malkavians are
essentially a whole new clan, but combined with the !Malks, they have some
really good, cheap vampires (it is very easy to assemble a reasonably sized
crypt that consists of nothing but vampires with DEM).

> people need to buy them.

I dunno. The Cam set strikes me as very solid. Sure, we didn't buy a ton of
it, but between the pre-release, a local booster draft tournament, and
simply picking up packs, each of about 6 solid local players bought at least
a box of boosters each. Which seems like a reasonable amount of sales.

> 15 new cards, or some of the vampires, had been significantly better
> than the old stuff, I think it would have sold better because you
> would have to buy Camarilla cards or lose your edge to those that did.

That would have been very bad--purposefully obsoleting previous stuff is bad
game design and bad marketing. Sure, it might make a few extra bucks, but it
deeply alienates your player base (well, unless you player base is stupid.
Please see the Heroclix BBS at www.hcrealms.com for a great example of a
deeply stupid player base...) The Camarilla set seems to be selling
fine--everyone around here bought as much of the Cam set as any other, if
not more. The new vampires are cool, there are very good reprints (Freak,
2nd, Apportation), and the starters work very well for sealed.

My opinion, but I'm pretty sure of myself about it. And frankly, I agree
with Peter Bakija's point that simply making the new cards more powerful
in order to sell more new cards is problematic to game balance. New cards
should be of comparable power to existing cards to whatever extent the
designers can manage to do that - understanding the whole process of
design and playtest is inexact, controversial, and subjective. And due to
the strange rarity problem caused by salting a print run that's basically
full of reprints with only a few new cards, I actually think it would have
been a *very* poor time to design any kind of "power" card of any sort.
The *LAST* thing I'd want to see is one new power rare card worth $30+ on
EBAY printed up at a rate of one pack per every three boxes of mostly
reprints that most players don't even need! Super-rare power cards are a
terrible thing!

As for how White Wolf views current, I only brought it up because I'm
sure the real thing that's holding sales back, not the quality of the new
cards or the vampires but the preponderance of reprints, was something
they had control over and presumably made a deliberate strategic decision
about. In short, it was the executives, not the card designers, who did
the whatever deed got done.

Fred

More veteran players, sure. But, CE is not any old expansion. It's a new base
set. There are a few losers that could have been omitted to make room for a
few more cards, but there's a definite limit if you want to retain the design
philosophy of it being a new Camarilla base set.

I maintain that no one likes new base sets (at least for CCGs that don't rotate
cards out of the environment). New players are still behind the collection
curve while veterans only want new cards. The more new cards you put in, the
more you screw the newbie who doesn't have sufficient access to the unreprinted
cards. The less, the more the veteran player scoffs at spending money on cards
already owned.

What was done with CE was a reasonable (probably near optimal) compromise.
Reprint most of the library stuff so that everyone has Majestys, Telepathic
Misdirections, et al which work with vampires from any set and do completely
new vampires that don't work with the originals to give a reason for the
veterans to buy the set while eliminating all of the issues with deciding which
vampires to reprint as well as the problem of newbies getting shafted by not
having accumulated the originals.

If you think CE should have been done differently, okay, but how would you
solve the problem of newbies and veterans having different interests? This
question is essential to why CE has a number of the features that it does,
which, in turn, affects why people may or may not want to buy it.

I think this view of things compares "new base sets" with a situation where older
base sets are still available, like we've got now...and assuming you don't view
the manner in which the older base sets are available to be a drawback. Personally,
I don't. But then, I'm all wired and find it easy to order up boxes from Potomac
or someone online when I want them. WW may feel that a new base set has a better
chance of being on actual store shelves (in a few stores, anyway) and thus actually
have a chance of bring new players into the game. And to get back to my original
point, having a new base set ultimately has to be compared to having to no base set
at all - which is really bad. You have to assume that someday, all those boxes of
Jyhad and VtES we've seen being sold cheap will go away. Of course, whether CE was
really needed this year might something to question if that's what the issue is.

Why is not just putting *all* reprints not the optimal thing? Why do we need
any new cards at all in what is otherwise basically a reprint set? New players
don't really them if all they're doing is getting caught up on owning staple
cards. My problem with the relatively small number of new cards in a set full
of reprints is that it creates high demand cards that both older and newer
players can use in a vast population of cards that only newer players can use.
That has the practical effect of making such cards seem more rare than their
true rarity level in the set in which they got printed. Rare new cards in a
set of reprints in particular "feel" like super-rares because everyone wants
them but only newer player have the full incentive to buy packs in this set.

In truth, I suspect the new cards in the set (and the new cards in Sabbat Wars,
the other example of this) probably served the function of creating interest in
the set. Older players may not need to buy any (or many) packs out of such a
set but at least they're keenly aware of it because of the new cards. The
awareness likely sells packs of cards one way or another, if only by giving the
feel of a more dynamic game. (I note these new cards in CE will be the only
changes to the game between last Christmas and whenever Anarchs finally come
out.) I don't like it, personally, but I guess I understand it. My ideal
compromise for this would be to avoid the new cards being rare. In fact,
lowering the intended rarity level for all the new cards (rare to uncommon,
uncommon to common, commmon maybe to common 2) would be helpful in these cases.

Messages.Body:
Curevei wrote:

>
> I could be facetious and say - then it's not a *new* base set but an old one.

It's a new base set for the same reason each new version of Magic the Gathering
is a new base set: there's a new combination of older cards being reprinted
together. They swap out some cards and swap in other cards that had only seen
printing in an expansion up until now (whether or not that expansion had been
printed before or after the last base set makes no nevermind) or even stuff that
had been in a base set but wasn't in the last one. Not new cards. But a new
*set* of cards.

Anyway, this is all semantics. Not that important.

> But, basically, it comes down to putting out sets that have some hope of making
> money. You have to give some reason for people to buy every set.

But you have to distinguish between groups of players. Older players who've got
original versions of all the reprints don't have much reason to buy a new base
set anyway. So why throw a few new cards in just to irritate them and make them
wade through a bunch of stuff they don't need just to get a effectively small
return on their investment? And newer players don't have the reprints so don't
care if the cards in the base set are reprints or not. One card they don't have
in a set is just as good as another.

I know it's ultimately not that cut and dried. I'm just explaining why I don't
think the concept of a few new cards in a set dominated by reprints can
accurately be termed, "optimal". Actually, "problematic" is more my word for
it.

> Whether you liked or even heard of Wheel of Time or not, the reason it died
> wasn't because it didn't sell but because distributors didn't approve of a new
> base set that was mostly reprints which delayed the production* of any product
> past the dreaded "unsupported point".
>

> plans and we started working on a set that was going to be 50% or so new.

> original set was largely unavailable. Could have done an expansion (everyone
> wanted) with new precons which would have sufficed to tide things over. This
> was possible due to the original base set being full of crap.

Sure. I think there's a few other issues here besides the optimal makeup of a
new base set, though: the original base set being bad and unavailable, distributor
interests diverging from manufacturer interests, unfortunate delays in making
crucial decisions. But I guess you're saying the same thing I said at the end
of my last post: whatever the optimal makeup of a base set is for player
purposes, other kinds of practical, real-world issues will often intrude on it.
